newsitem.title: DENMARK: East Asia gas demand to double to 300 bcm by 2010.
newsitem.headline: East Asia gas demand to double to 300 bcm by 2010.

text.p: COPENHAGEN, June 12, Reuter - Natural gas demand in East Asia will double to around 300 billion cubic metres (bcm) a year from a current 140 bcm year by 2010, Koshiro Goda, vice president of the Japan Gas Association, told the World Gas Conference here on Thursday.

"On the one hand its utilisation as an electric power generation fuel is expected to increase. On the other hand, its employment as a resource in the manufacture of chemicals and fertilisers as well as a fuel for industrial purposes is anticipated to burgeon," he said.
At present Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) accounts for 70 bcm a year of the total, or 53 million tonnes, while pipeline gas supplies 74 bcm, he added.

Trading is expected to increase as pipeline gas grows, he said. Malaysia, Indonesia, Myanmar and Vietnam are all developing their industries, but only Malaysia and Singapore are now involved in trade, Goda said.
"A pipeline from Myanmar to Thailand is now under construction and trade in natural gas between these two countries is expected to commence in the near future," he said.

Construction of international pipelines as well as closer economic ties between ASEAN (Association of South East Asian Nations) is expected to result in the development of a pipeline network covering the whole region, Goda added.
"Attention should also be given to future supply resources, such as a pipeline from Eastern Siberia, which is currently creating some debate," he said.
Rem Vyakhirev, chairman of Russia's Gazprom, on Wednesday told the conference that Russia was looking to start selling gas to East Asia early next century.

But while pipeline gas use grows, LNG will remain vital. Goda said that Japan, Korea and Taiwan will all expand LNG imports, and Thailand, India, China and other countries will start importing LNG to augment existing domestic production of gas.

A competitive market is vital to help natural gas use grow, he said. As European and US gas have become cheaper in recent years with their markets becoming more competitive, "it is essential that natural gas maintains its competitive edge if it is to be chosen as the most appropriate energy source by the Asian market."
Energy demand growth reflects the astonishing growth in the region of both GDP and population, Goda said.

In 1990 Asia's GDP was $4.7 trillion, compared with $6.4 trillion for the EU and $6.3 for NAFTA. By 1995 Asia had risen to $8.1 trillion, compared with $7.8 trillion for NAFTA and $8.4 trillion for the EU. And population is expected to grow to 3.6 billion by 2010 from 2.9 billion now. --Sebastian Alison, Copenhagen Newsroom, +45 33 96 96 50
